title: The Double Flash
subtitle: The Vela Incident · Indian Ocean, 1979
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, the remote Southern Indian Ocean near the Prince Edward Islands in September 1979, vast empty grey-blue sea under heavy overcast, sub-Antarctic cold, occasional drifting icebergs on the horizon, an early satellite-control-room interior with CRT screens and 1970s mainframes, melancholy and uncanny, period 1979 detail, cinematic wide composition, fine film grain, no text, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: In September nineteen seventy-nine, an American satellite detected a double flash of light, over the southern Indian Ocean.
beats.img: A vast empty grey-blue Southern Ocean under heavy overcast with a faint distant double flash of light reflecting off low cloud cover, cold sub-Antarctic light, eerie, no people, no horizon detail.

beats.vo: A double flash is the signature of a nuclear weapon. The brief, intense initial flash. The second, expanding fireball.
beats.cap:
The signature
of a nuclear test
beats.img: A vintage 1970s American satellite-control-room console with CRT screens and rows of indicator lamps, dim fluorescent light, paper strip charts, documentary still, eerie, no people.

beats.vo: Forty years of scholarship lean toward a joint test, by two governments that have never confirmed it.
beats.img: A remote sub-Antarctic volcanic island silhouette against a heavy grey ocean horizon at dusk, hazy fading light, cold empty sea, desolate and remote, no people.

beats.vo: The United States has never reclassified the event. The file remains, officially, ambiguous.
beats.img: An empty grey ocean at night under a starless overcast sky, vast and featureless, a single distant indistinct shape on the horizon fading into darkness, melancholy and unresolved, no people.
